metrics.brief: make a website for my cousin's clothing boutique called Thread & Loom in Pune. it sells handloom kurtas, sarees, cotton shirts and dupattas. people should be able to browse products by category, filter by size and price, see a size guide, check new arrivals, and order on whatsapp. also show a lookbook section with styled outfits, the store timings and location, the return and exchange policy, and a few customer reviews. it should feel earthy and elegant and work well on phones

raises.why: the Requester's answer: go with option 1

review.verdict: The department collected a solid brief and charter, then shipped nothing: it stalled on a budget gap (80 against a rate-card floor of 110), spent 0 of 80, built no site (0 bytes), and no workflow was ever proposed, priced or registered.

identity.note: Strong on intake: two question rounds [2][5] produced a 12-item charter with nothing to be confirmed, and the validator accepted it [10]. Weak on the limit. At [19] it offered the Requester only 'Finish as it is', although the rules also allow dropping items and Adaptation had proposed a drop list [18]. [12] and [19] describe the result as 'the site as it is now, with 1 thing still not right' when metrics show nothing was built. [22] promises 'a last check' that never happened (Audit had 0 turns). [17] told Adaptation to cover all 12 items after Adaptation had said that was impossible [11].

adaptation.note: It did the cost arithmetic and gave a recommendation, but never wrote a proposal, so there was nothing for Priority to price [11][18]. It also made a budget-affordability call, which belongs to Priority. Its drop list mislabels items: it calls items 1, 9 and 12 'styling items', but 9 is the store address and hours, and 12 is the no-JS-errors and no-overflow gate. Its trade-off line omits losing the store section. Its first recommendation (drop 12, 9, 1, then 10) differs from the second (drop 1, 9, 12, 8, 11) with no explanation. It also asked for '30 more units' when the budget was already at the cap of 80.

priority.note: 0 turns, so it was never tested. The flow let Adaptation judge affordability before Priority saw any proposal. Not a role breach by Priority, but it contributed nothing.

coordination.note: 0 turns. With 0 registered workflows there was nothing to schedule, so this is expected. Not tested.

audit.note: 0 turns, with nothing built to check. Identity's promise of a final check [22] was not backed by any Audit turn.

went_well: Identity gathered every fact in two rounds and recorded rules that prevent invented content (no sale items, placeholder images, WhatsApp-only orders). [2][5][10]
Charter done-when items are specific and checkable (exact products, prices, sizes, address, reviews). Validator passed it with 12 items. [10]
Identity did not ask the Requester until the limit was hit, and the budget raise 40 to 80 was logged cleanly. [15]
Zero redirects, invalid moves, role refusals or stuck loops. The run was cheap: 11 AI calls, 6.7 minutes.
problems: No workflow, grant, build or audit occurred, so the department's core loop (J2.b to J2.h) was never exercised.

The department treated the rate-card minimum (110) as a hard floor and never tested a cheaper path. Bundling was 'rejected' [18] with no named source or check. Unverified: actual cost is unknown because spent is 0.
The final Requester choice [19] was missing the 'drop items' option, so the Requester picked between an empty site and nothing. A 7-item build for 75 was on the table [18].
Wording to the Requester hid the real state: 'site as it is now' versus site_bytes 0, and 'nothing has been checked yet' for something that did not exist. [12][19][22]
Adaptation mislabelled done-when items 9 and 12, and its drop recommendation would remove the store section and the quality gate while keeping policy.
learnings: Change: when the budget is below the floor, require Identity to offer the Requester 'drop items' as well as 'add budget' and 'ship as is', with the drop list stated. Evidence: [18][19].

Change: make Adaptation submit a proposal for the affordable subset and let Priority return GRANT, COUNTER or REFUSE. Evidence: Priority 0 turns, proposals 0, and Adaptation made the affordability call itself [11][18].
Change the test system: when nothing was built, the Requester-facing text must say 'the site is empty'. Evidence: site_bytes 0 against the wording in [12][19].
Change the test system: give the state a short label for each done-when item so cost talk cannot mislabel them. Evidence: items 9 and 12 called 'styling' [18].

Test next: run the same brief at a budget of 120 or more, and once at 80 with a drop list forced, and compare 'estimate_vs_charged' with the rate-card minimums. This run has no charged data, so the 110 floor is unverified.
Check the scenario: a cap of 80 against a 110 floor made this run unwinnable by design. If the aim was to test limit handling, keep it, but label it that way. It says nothing about build quality.
Keep: the two-round intake and charter rules. Evidence is thin beyond that, since only intake and the limit path ran, and Priority, Coordination, Audit and the workflow agents are untested.

events.detail: Adaptation asked: Budget is 40 and the minimum cost to cover all 12 done-when items is 110. Recommendation: ask the Requester to raise the budget to about 110, which keeps the full brief. If they will not, drop items in this order: 12 (styling), 9 (styling), 1 (styling), then 10 (policy section), keeping the core shop (items 2, 3, 4, 7, 5, 6). Even then the floor is about 85, so the Requester must still choose between more budget and a smaller site. Trade-off: a smaller site ships the lookbook, store details, policy and reviews later or not at all. Which does Identity rule, and what is the new budget?
40 -> 80 (asked +40, cap 80; the Requester's answer: go with option 1)
